Sergei Rachmaninoff. A Russian composer, virtuoso pianist and conductor who was one of the last great champions of late Romanticism in classical music.

Possessing legendary technical ability and unusually large hands, Rachmaninoff wrote some of the most challenging and expressive piano music in the repertoire, characterized by sweeping melodies, rich harmonies, and bell-like tolling chords. Following the Russian Revolution of 1917, he fled Russia and spent the remainder of his life in exile in the West, working primarily as a touring concert pianist.

His most celebrated work is Piano Concerto No. 2 in C minor, Opus 18, completed in 1901. It was written to mark his recovery from a severe three-year depression and writer's block using hypnotherapy by Doctor Nikolai Dahl, to whom the piece is dedicated. The Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini, Opus 43, from 1934, is a concertante work for piano and orchestra consisting of twenty-four variations on Paganini's Caprice No. 24. It features a famous, soaring eighteenth variation that is a melodic inversion of Paganini's original theme.

Piano Concerto No. 3 in D minor, Opus 30, completed in 1909, is famously dubbed the Rach 3. It's widely feared by pianists as one of the most technically demanding and physically exhausting concertos in the classical canon. The Prelude in C-sharp minor, Opus 3, No. 2, was written in 1892 when Rachmaninoff was just nineteen. This dramatic solo piano work became so popular worldwide that audiences demanded he play it as an encore at nearly every recital, much to his eventual frustration.

Symphony No. 2 in E minor, Opus 27, completed in 1907, is a grand, lushly romantic symphony that restored his confidence in symphonic writing after the disastrous premiere of his Symphony No. 1 in 1897, which had been poorly conducted by a reputedly intoxicated Alexander Glazunov.

The Bells, Opus 35, from 1913, is a choral symphony setting a Russian translation of Edgar Allan Poe's poem of the same name, representing four stages of life. Silver sleigh bells represent youth, golden wedding bells represent marriage, brass alarm bells represent danger, and iron mourning bells represent death. Tchaikovsky acted as a mentor to the young Rachmaninoff, championing his graduation opera Aleko and heavily influencing his melodic style.
